thread.title: Ignore Trader Noise, Buy QQQ Now - Invesco QQQ ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ)

author: Kirk Spano
title: Ignore Trader Noise, Buy QQQ Now - Invesco QQQ ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ)
text:
Three months ago I was telling you to start selling stocks . By my 4th Quarter Macro And Market Outlook (Editor's Pick) in early October, I said this:
"I am holding about 25% cash in portfolios because...risk is high."
Over the past three weeks I have been scaling back into stocks again despite all the breathy talk to become a seller from talking heads and traders.
While I appreciate the narrative that there has been some technical damage done to the stock market, I think most technical analysts don't understand their own charts.
There are technical, quantitative and fundamental reasons to be a stock buyer now, if even for a swing trade. But, there is also reason to buy now because if news is positive on trade in the next couple weeks and the Fed minutes come off a just a bit more dovish, we could actually see a substantial melt-up in the stock market and get the euphoria I discussed over a year ago:
Let's Get Technical Traders have rightly pointed out that there is technical damage to the market. However, they have focused on shorter term trends. It is easy to see that longer term trends up and to the right are still intact for now.
Here's a longer-term technical chart of the PowerShares QQQ ETF ( QQQ ), which I maintain is the best diversified index.
For long-term trends, I like to watch the 1, 2 and 5 year weekly exponential moving averages (which are slightly more weighted heavily towards the near-term versus simple moving averages). I pay special attention to the 2-year for market support.
I want to see the $155.34 level hold this week. That is important in my view as the larger cyclical support for the bull market starts much further down at $128.14.
The S&P 500 ( SPY ) ( VOO ) looks like this:
As you can see, the uptrend is still intact, but flirting with 2-year support. I'd like to see the S&P 500 not fall below $2587.
Remember, no technical analysis is perfect. In my experience, simpler and longer-term in nature is most effective for investors. Traders need more bells and whistles, but as I'll explain below, technical traders are at the mercy of today's quant traders anyway.
For long-term investors, the short-term trends have not confirmed any breaks in the long-term trends as yet. For now, long-term investors should not be sellers. Those with cash though, I believe should be scaling into certain new equity positions.
It is a trap for investors who are focused on the long-term to worry about the shorter-term trends until major long-term supports are broken. In fact, these short term corrections so breathlessly narrated by traders are the right time for long-term investors to add more to their equity holdings. I would venture a guess that @BuyandHold2012 is buying stocks or has been recently.
Valuations Are Almost Normal The main way to value the stock market is based upon price to earnings ratio. Recently, forward PE ratios were much higher. The correction and further stock buybacks have changed that equation quite a bit.
Source: Thomson Reuters Datastream as of 11/19/18 via Deutsche Bank
Further, while many like to point out that the CAPE Shiller PE Ratio is quite a bit higher at about 35. The ten-year average PE is 16.179 according to Yale data as of October 2018. We will see how much lower it is in a week. If the above forward estimate for PE is roughly correct for 2019, then the market is roughly fairly valued.
And here is a question I would have for the chart above: what if interest rates chop along near current levels for an extended period? I think the answer is that CAPE would drift down as earnings slowly rose on reduced share counts.
I'd point out that the Bianco PE Ratio which accounts for total return by factoring in dividends, is more line line with the forward looking estimate. Here is a comparison from June (if anybody has a link to current Bianco PE I'd love for you to include it in the comments, I am awaiting reply from DWS regarding future access) :
You can see the dramatic difference in PE smoothing devices. The Bianco PE was much closer to its 10-year average than the Shiller pre-correction.
Fundamentals Are Good In The New Economy Here I will mention Jeff Miller before I run through things in a bullet point list, his Weighing the Week Ahead is a must read for the regular indicators he follows, as well as, his insights. Particularly, look at the recession indicators. There is no recession in sight for at least the next few quarters.
The strengths of the economy are many, in particular strong employment numbers and small business development. Here are some leading indicators:
"Economic activity in the manufacturing sector expanded in October, and the overall economy grew for the 114th consecutive month, say the nation’s supply executives in the latest Manufacturing ISM ® Report On Business ® ... The October PMI ® registered 57.7 percent, a decrease of 2.1 percentage points from the September reading of 59.8 percent. The New Orders Index registered 57.4 percent, a decrease of 4.4 percentage points from the September reading of 61.8 percent. The Production Index registered 59.9 percent, a 4 -percentage point decrease compared to the September reading of 63.9 percent. The Employment Index registered 56.8 percent, a decrease of 2 percentage points from the September reading of 58.8 percent. The Supplier Deliveries Index registered 63.8 percent, a 2.7-percentage point increase from the September reading of 61.1 percent. The Inventories Index registered 50.7 percent, a decrease of 2.6 percentage points from the September reading of 53.3 percent. The Prices Index registered 71.6 percent, a 4.7-percentage point increase from the September reading of 66.9 percent, indicating higher raw materials prices for the 32nd consecutive month. - ISM My takeaway here is that manufacturing remained strong, but did experience a mild slow down. It will be interesting to watch inventory numbers through and after the holidays. Tight inventories would be an indicator that manufacturing would pick up again soon. U.S. homebuilding rose in October on strength in multifamily which was up 15%, although single family building fell for a second month. Interest rates are the named culprit in the single family slow down. Multifamily showed renewed strength and I believe we are still in the early innings of expansion in multifamily. New projects in Queens and Northern Virginia on heels Amazon's ( AMZN ) HQ2 announcement should keep multifamily rising short-term. There were 13 multifamily projects of over $100 million reported in October. And some lagging indicators:
The unemployment rate is at 3.7% which is very good, though Millennial men are still not participating as they should be due to a significant skills gap. The labor participation rate is 62.9% and relatively stable the past 5 years. Approximately 500,000 men ages 25-34 are not in the labor force despite being able bodied, indicating some more slack in the labor market is available. That in turn indicates to me that the Fed could be less aggressive given wages have barely budged . Retail sales continue to be strong, as is, consumer confidence. Inflation remains low giving the Fed more room to be less hawkish than people fear. Finally, earnings growth on the back of stable to slightly rising revenues, as well as, big buybacks in the "new economy" stocks gives the entire market a buoyancy that traders will have a hard time overcoming. Reports are coming in that buybacks for 2019 will exceed the record amount of 2018.
Despite concerns about wage and wealth inequality that are real and will come to a head eventually, the economy continues to be resilient even if exceptional growth numbers are no longer apparent - something I have pointed out is "normal" in the " slow growth forever " economy.
I discussed the slow growth forever economy in a September free Friday webinar, along with my market outlook:
But Risks Persist There are four key fears I have for the economy and markets:
The Fed remains aggressive and we see an inverted yield curve. I believe the long-end of the curve is telegraphing that growth will be slow, it is important that the Fed get that message. Trade concerns centered on the United States and China. Should the trade war escalate, the world's two largest economies almost certainly slow down by H2 next year in a way that could lead us into recession by 2020. European economic problems cause a bank failures in 2019 which spill over despite the ECB's best efforts. Oil prices do not adhere to the apparent ceiling around $80 per barrel and shoot through that level causing inflation. There are more risks of course, both known and unknown, however, these are the four I see as most concerning and that could have the most impact. Think of how NASA monitors the risk of earth impacts by space objects.
The risks I listed have varying degrees of likelihood and potential impact on the economy. The Fed seems to be the most likely to have a large negative impact. Oil prices, though I expect to rise, I think aren't likely to rise high enough to damage the economy - I discussed the Goldilocks price for oil here .
Buy QQQ In summary, I believe the risks have been largely priced into the stock market and positive catalysts have been ignored the past month. As I discussed with Brian Bain in an interview, I believe the " new economy " leads for many years to come.
The "new economy" is largely held within the lightly diversified NASDAQ 100. The PowerShares QQQ ETF ( QQQ ) is my favorite for tracking the mature portion of the "new economy." It is slightly over 60% technology, with slugs of consumer discretionary and healthcare.
Given the new arrangement of the sectors per Standard and Poor's I do prefer QQQ to any combination of technology ETFs with other ETFs at this point, as QQQ still holds Google ( GOOG ) and several other recategorized companies.

I did a much deeper dive into QQQ here:
ETF File: The Only ETF You Need To Start Investing
QQQ is catching a bid on Monday, making it less likely that it will pierce the support levels discussed at the opening. I am a buyer of QQQ at these levels.
If the risk factors I have listed above develop into problems, and support is broken, then we would need to rethink our asset allocations. For now, I still recommend working up to at least 25% of a portfolio in QQQ and/or certain QQQ stocks. My allocation is approximately 38% as of today.
